tier_reason: Upgraded from C: jrsonnet's docs/benchmarks.adoc is an independent measurement (by a competing implementation's author) of Sjsonnet 0.6.2 native/GraalVM release binaries against google/jsonnet (C++) and go-jsonnet v0.22.0-rc1, with public harness code (nix/benchmarks.nix, hyperfine -N -w4 -m20, inputs from jrsonnet tests/realworld and google/jsonnet perf_tests/benchmarks) and the CPU stated (AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D). Not A because compiler versions and flags for the C++/Go builds are not stated (nix stdenv defaults) and sjsonnet is a prebuilt binary.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Independent (jrsonnet docs/benchmarks.adoc, Sjsonnet 0.6.2 Scala Native binary run per process like the others): real-world GraalVM CI 69.6 ms vs go-jsonnet 600.3 ms (about 8.6x, derived from page data) and kube-prometheus 204.6 ms vs 1068.4 ms (about 5.2x, derived); google/jsonnet C++ was not timed on these because it 'takes longer than a hour'. Where C++ ran, Sjsonnet native was faster on every case, e.g. Large string join 9.7 vs 39.7 ms (4.1x), Simple recursive call 18.0 vs 78.8 ms (4.4x), Tail call 2406.8 vs 18460.1 ms (7.7x), Inheritance recursion 46.7 vs 1216.9 ms (26x), Big object 3756.8 vs 16199.6 ms (4.3x) (ratios derived from page data). First-party README (18 May 2023, internal Databricks file staging/runbot-app.jsonnet, ~6.6 MB output): Sjsonnet 0.4.3 ~0.10 s vs go-jsonnet 0.20.0 ~6.5 s vs google/jsonnet 0.20.0 ~67 s (about 65x and 670x, derived from page data), with Sjsonnet run as a warm long-lived daemon and the others as subprocesses.
corrections.hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D 16-core (jrsonnet docs/benchmarks.adoc); README 2023 numbers state no hardware
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Sjsonnet 0.6.2 prebuilt release binaries (Scala Native and GraalVM native-image) wrapped with --max-stack 200000; google/jsonnet built with its own Makefile defaults and go-jsonnet with nixpkgs buildGoModule (nix/cpp-jsonnet.nix, nix/go-jsonnet.nix); compiler versions not stated
corrections.caveats: The README's 65x/670x figures are first-party (May 2023, Sjsonnet 0.4.3) on an internal Databricks config that cannot be reproduced, and compare a warm JVM daemon with cold subprocesses for go-jsonnet and google/jsonnet, so they overstate the like-for-like gap. The independent jrsonnet runs (per-process CLI for all) give smaller margins: about 5-9x over go-jsonnet on real-world configs, and the C++ reference was too slow to time on real-world inputs. Sjsonnet is not uniformly faster than go-jsonnet: it is slower on Big object (3756.8 vs 2544.5 ms), Inheritance function recursion (2394.1 vs 1414.3 ms), std.manifestJsonEx (2443.6 vs 1426.9 ms), std.manifestTomlEx (2558.8 vs 1427.7 ms) and std.parseInt (2383.6 vs 1398.2 ms). The Rust implementation jrsonnet beats Sjsonnet on most cases (GraalVM CI 2.0x, kube-prometheus 4.7x per jrsonnet's table; Sjsonnet's own docs/perf-gap-vs-jrsonnet.md, 2026-05-13 on an Apple M3 Pro, still shows kube-prometheus 1.68x behind jrsonnet). The benchmark is run by a competitor; compiler versions for the C++/Go builds are unstated, and the mimir real-world case skipped Sjsonnet (databricks/sjsonnet issue #829). JVM startup adds about 1 s per invocation for the plain JAR (client-server mode cuts it to 0.2-0.3 s per the README).

notes: README numbers match exactly; tier raised to B on jrsonnet's independent public-harness benchmark, which also shows jrsonnet (Rust, not in the catalog yet, a possible lead) is faster than Sjsonnet on most workloads. Category: language-interpreters fits (Jsonnet evaluator compared with other evaluators); if a data-format category is preferred, the nearest earlier-wave one is json. Metadata confirmed on github.com: Apache-2.0, 318 stars, not archived or a fork, last commit 2026-09-28.

tier_reason: First-party README table generated by the public d5/tengobench harness (cmd/bench/main.go, code/fib.*), but no hardware, Go version or flags are stated and the table was last regenerated in May 2020; C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: fib(35), one timed run per interpreter including process start: Tengo 2,315 ms vs go-lua 4,028 ms (1.7x, derived from page data), GopherLua 4,409 ms (1.9x, derived), goja 5,194 ms, starlark-go 6,954 ms, gpython 11,324 ms, Yaegi 11,715 ms, otto 48,539 ms, Anko 52,821 ms. Reference rows on the same page are faster than Tengo: native Lua 756 ms (about 3.1x faster, derived) and native Python 2 1,907 ms. fibt(35) is startup-dominated and shows no win: Tengo 3 ms ties go-lua, GopherLua and starlark-go (3 ms), native Lua is 2 ms.
corrections.caveats: Single recursive microbenchmark in the project's own README. The harness (d5/tengobench cmd/bench/main.go) times one os/exec run per interpreter with process start included and ignores exit errors (_ = cmd.Run()), so a failing interpreter would show a tiny time; no repetitions or output checks. The table dates from tengobench's 'update output' commit of 2 May 2020 (tengo v2.1.2, go 1.14 in go.mod) and has not been refreshed since; hardware, Go version and flags are not stated. Native Lua 5.x (756 ms) and native Python 2 (1,907 ms) are faster than Tengo (2,315 ms), so Tengo beats other Go-hosted interpreters, not the C implementations that are the category's baselines. fibt(35) only measures startup.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly; the record's 'fibt: Tengo 3 ms vs Yaegi 10 ms' was cherry-picked (three other Go interpreters tie at 3 ms), corrected. Better category fit is embedded-scripting (same wave 12; Tengo is an embeddable Go scripting language whose comparators are GopherLua, goja and go-lua), not an earlier wave; GopherLua and goja are separate wave 12 entries. Metadata confirmed: MIT, 3.8k stars, not archived or a fork, last commit 2026-10-03.

tier_reason: Upgraded from D: the numbers behind the README claim are on github.com in PR #88 (merged 2022-01-31), a first-party table from the public harness scripts/benchmark_awks.py over testdata/tt.* comparing GoAWK with one-true-awk, gawk and mawk; no hardware, Go version or awk versions stated, so C.

corrections.baseline: one-true-awk (original-awk), gawk and mawk; also GoAWK's previous tree-walking interpreter ('orig')
corrections.claimed_speedup: PR #88 real-world table (speed relative to one-true-awk = 1.00, 23 testdata/tt.* scripts): geo mean GoAWK 1.45, GoAWK tree-walker 1.28, gawk 1.86, mawk 2.32. GoAWK beats one-true-awk on 18 of 23 scripts but is slower on tt.04 (0.97), tt.05 (0.95), tt.10 (0.34), tt.10a (0.32) and tt.15 (0.62); it beats gawk on 9 of 23. By geo mean gawk is about 1.28x and mawk about 1.6x faster than GoAWK (derived from page data). README: 'Most AWK scripts are faster than awk and on a par with gawk, though usually slower than mawk.'
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers from January 2022 (bytecode VM PR #88); hardware, OS, Go version and awk versions are not stated. Harness scripts/benchmark_awks.py takes the minimum of runs 2-6 of six per awk, repeats the input file until GoAWK runs at least 0.5 s, includes process start and does not compare outputs across awks. The README's 'on a par with gawk' is generous against its own data (gawk geo mean 1.86 vs GoAWK 1.45), mawk is faster on every script, and regex-heavy scripts are slower than other awks because of Go's regexp package (README). The linked blog article (benhoyt.com/writings/goawk-compiler-vm) is blocked here; a search snippet shows the same geo means (goawk 1.45, orig 1.28, awk 1.00, gawk 1.86).

notes: Tier raised D to C: numbers found in PR #88 on github.com; GoAWK is faster than one-true-awk only, slower than gawk and mawk by geo mean, so it is weak as a 'faster' entry (keep with that shortcoming). frawk, a faster AWK, is already in wave 12 merged; if the orchestrator prefers an earlier-wave category for AWK implementations, the nearest is text-search-and-indexing (grep-style text processing), with csv-tabular for its CSV mode. Metadata confirmed: MIT, 2.1k stars, not archived or a fork, last commit 2026-09-15 (v1.32.0), used in Redpanda Connect per README.
